title: Room-temperature tuning and probing of Fermi polarons in atomically thin semiconductors on a plasmonic metasurface
authors: Tingting Wu, Francesca Maria Marchetti, Antonio Tiene, Antonio I. Fernández-Domínguez, Miao Qi, Zhe Wang, Lin Liu, Lei Wei, Francisco J. Garcia-Vidal, Mengxiao Chen, Qi Jie Wang, Yu Luo
abstract: The Fermi polaron, arising from interactions between a mobile impurity and a degenerate Fermi sea, is a many-body quasiparticle that provides a sensitive probe of strongly correlated electronic phases in atomically thin semiconductors. In doped transition-metal dichalcogenides, the attractive and repulsive polaron branches are well established in monolayers. However, extending active control and quantitative, branch-resolved probing to stacked geometries has remained elusive because spectral quenching and weak optical contrast restrict access to Fermi polaron signatures. Here, we integrate electron-doped WS$_2$ flakes from monolayer to quadrilayer with a strain-tunable plasmonic metasurface, enabling high-contrast scattering readout at room temperature through coupling between Fermi polaron resonances and surface plasmons. This platform enables quantitative extraction of polaron branch spectral weights and coupling strengths across different layer numbers. We uncover a systematic thickness dependence of the spectral-weight distribution and demonstrate continuous and fully reversible spectral-weight transfer between attractive and repulsive branches in bilayers and quadrilayers, with near-complete transfer achieved in bilayers. By identifying layer number and strain as complementary control parameters for Fermi polarons, our results establish metasurface-enabled scattering spectroscopy as a practical route to resolve and manipulate many-body resonances in stacked van der Waals semiconductors, bridging idealized monolayer polaron physics and device-relevant architectures.
summary: This research develops a novel platform combining atomically thin semiconductors ($	ext{WS}_2$) with plasmonic metasurfaces to study Fermi polarons at room temperature. By using scattering spectroscopy, the authors achieve quantitative control over polaron branch spectral weights by tuning both the film thickness and applying uniaxial strain. This establishes a powerful tool for manipulating correlated electronic states in 2D materials.
main_problem: The challenge is extending active, quantitative, branch-resolved probing of Fermi polarons (FPs) from monolayer to stacked geometries in atomically thin semiconductors.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that integrating $	ext{WS}_2$ with a plasmonic metasurface allows for room-temperature, strain-tunable spectroscopy to resolve and manipulate the attractive and repulsive polaron branches across multiple layers.
method: The study combines dark-field scattering spectroscopy measurements with theoretical modeling based on coupled oscillator Hamiltonians (COM) to fit spectral features.
model_or_system: The system involves electron-doped $	ext{WS}_2$ flakes (1L to 4L) placed on a strain-tunable plasmonic metasurface. The physics is modeled via the Fermi polaron quasiparticle interacting with the degenerate Fermi sea and coupled to surface plasmons, forming three hybrid polariton branches.
key_observables: Polaron branch spectral weights ($w_{AP}, w_{RP}$), Rabi coupling strength ($\Omega$), energy splitting between branches, and temperature dependence of these features.
important_parameters: Layer number (1L to 4L), applied uniaxial strain (tensile/compressive), electron doping level, and plasmonic resonance frequency.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes that the optical response in multilayer samples is dominated by the metal-proximal layer, simplifying the full vertical averaging problem. PL measurements are sometimes used as an independent benchmark for intrinsic parameters.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (metasurface integration), spectral evolution under strain and thickness changes, and theoretical fitting of coupled oscillator models to extract coupling strengths and spectral weights.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing a robust scattering spectroscopy technique that overcomes PL quenching in multilayers. It then systematically investigates how layer number controls the overall polaron response, culminating in demonstrating that uniaxial strain acts as a powerful knob to deterministically redistribute oscillator strength between the attractive and repulsive branches.
why_interesting: The work provides an excellent example of using plasmonics to enhance optical contrast for probing subtle many-body physics (FPs) in solid-state systems, bridging fundamental correlated electron theory with device-relevant heterostructures.
